claims.text: CALPHAD-based computational modeling can be used to control phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
CALPHAD-based computational modeling predicts phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
CALPHAD-based computational modeling predicts phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
The relevant material is in an initial, undeformed state.
The structural mediator is the set of constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations.
Ab initio or density-functional-theory calculations provide the mechanism for predicting phase stability and evolution.
The proposed intervention will result in controlled phase evolution.
Without the intervention, phase evolution is uncontrolled.
The effectiveness of the method is limited by computational-model accuracy and the availability of reliable input data.
The complexity of high-entropy-alloy systems and limited experimental validation create uncertainty in phase-stability and phase-evolution predictions.
Predicted phase evolution can be tested against experimental phase composition, microstructure, and mechanical properties for Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
A mismatch between predicted and experimentally observed phase evolution would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention is identified as CALPHAD modeling, but the mechanism is identified as ab initio or density-functional-theory calculations. These are distinct computational approaches; DFT may supply inputs to some thermodynamic models, but it is not itself the stated CALPHAD intervention. No relationship between them is explained.
